newsitem.title: FRANCE: Striking truckers maintain stranglehold on France.
newsitem.headline: Striking truckers maintain stranglehold on France.

text.p: Striking truck drivers maintained their 11-day-old stranglehold on the French economy Thursday, defying government pleas to return to work after talks with bosses broke down over pay demands.
But despite the deadlock and the truckers' 250 barricades throttling roads and fuel depots, all sides held out hopes for a settlement of the 11-day-old dispute.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe ruled out using force to clear the roadblocks, and Transport Minister Bernard Pons told television the door to a solution was open.
"I think there will be advances in the next hours," he said.
Employers said their rejected pay offer was "flexible." The national truckers' federation FNCR called for talks to resume.

The strike forced increasing petrol rationing, shut factories for lack of supplies and trapped hundreds of foreign trucks. The strikers relaxed a blockade at the Channel port of Calais to let stranded British trucks get on ferries for home.

Employers and unions are due to meet Friday morning to sign accords on demands already settled, including the right of truckers to retire at 55 after 25 years at the wheel, changes on sick pay and travel expenses, and a ban on trucks driving on weekends.

Major unions said strikers camped in trucks parked across chilly highways had voted to keep pressing their demands on pay and working hours, even though Pons said government mediator Robert Cros had successfully completed his mission.
"I think (the blockade) will go on for a while," said Roger Poletti of the Force Ouvriere (FO) union.
"Very positive results were obtained," Pons said.
Road haulage employers said their pay offer was open to amendment and urged truckers to end their blockade.
Jean-Louis Amato, president of the Unostra hauliers' association, said the offer of a 1 percent real pay rise and a 1,500 franc ($300) one-time bonus was "flexible."
Unions are demanding pay increases that amount to an average 23 percent. "We have made a big effort," said Rene Petit, speaking on behalf of the four employers' federations.
Pons said a group made up of representatives of unions and employers would try to tackle the issue of defining working hours for drivers.

"If this working group does not agree quickly, I will propose to the government that we settle the issue by decree," he said. Drivers say they often work more than 200 hours a month, with many hours unpaid waiting for loading and unloading.

The state traffic information centre counted 245 blockades on major highways at 5 p.m. (1600 GMT/11 a.m. EST) Thursday, slightly down from 247 on Wednesday. Snow and sleet fell overnight in some areas.
A two-day strike by airline crews added to travel problems.

Strikers completed a blockade of oil refineries, forming barricades outside the only one of 13 that had escaped the strike so far. About 5,000 of 18,000 petrol stations were either dry or feeling shortages, an industry ministry official said.

The roadblocks have forced the closures of some factories and cut supplies of perishable goods ranging from fish to fruit and flowers. Farmers reported shortages of animal feed as grain shipments were hit and the strike was also disrupting mail.
The French strike and an unrelated truckers' strike in Denmark caused problems in other European countries, clogging highways and ports and disrupting commerce.
